author: Sadie Harley
headline: Reusable molecular fabric could cut energy needed to separate industrial chemicals
text: Separating out a particular toxic chemical from industrial processes linked to the manufacture of nylon, paint, certain foams found in furniture and even detergents requires a lot of energy and hassle. Now a team of scientists from UT Austin and Zhejiang University has struck upon a solution that could prove far more energy efficient and practical. The research is published in the journal Nature. Companies often use a chemical called cyclohexane in making a range of materials, but cyclohexane is typically produced from a similarly shaped chemical called benzene, which is a carcinogen. When chemists create cyclohexane, they often form toxic benzene as an additional, unwanted product, and the process for separating the two is highly energy-intensive. The researchers' solution involves a molecularly woven fabric that can filter out most of the benzene in a mixture. 'Unbelievable amounts of energy go into chemical separation. It's one of the top energy sinks in the modern world,' said UT chemist Jonathan Sessler, one of the corresponding authors on the paper. 'In a sense, we are addressing the challenge of improving efficiency using one of humanity's oldest technologies: weaving. It's remarkable that the same principle of interlacing works at the molecular level.' Similar boiling points complicate separation: Chemical plants traditionally separate cyclohexane from benzene by using a distillation method. Different chemicals have different boiling points, so in many cases chemists can heat a mixture up until the unwanted chemicals vaporize, leaving the necessary ones behind or vice versa. However, cyclohexane and benzene have nearly the same boiling points and tend to vaporize together. This complicates the distillation process and typically requires the addition of additives. 'This makes traditional distillation-based benzene-cyclohexane separations challenging and expensive,' said Sessler, the R.P. Doherty, Jr.-Welch Regents Chair in Chemistry. Molecular networks weave themselves into a filter: The new fabric is made of four molecular networks that weave above and below each other to create a layer with an interlocking pattern. A single layer of the material can come in two forms: one in which the various molecular networks cross each other in a clockwise spiral and a mirror-like version in which the networks cross in a counterclockwise spiral. This property is known as chirality or 'handedness.' To create the fabric, layers are stacked on top of each other, alternating between the regular orientation and the mirror-image orientation. This creates a springy fabric that can act as a thick filter, separating large amounts of benzene from cyclohexane. The multithread fabric is stronger than linearly woven fabric, where single threads are woven to make a layer. The new fabric is self-assembling, meaning that the molecular networks arrange and interconnect on their own. 'The whole thing converges by itself based on the underlying chemistry, which is especially cool because it allows the creation of these new materials in a facile way,' Sessler said. Reusable fabric absorbs 97.9% of benzene: The fabric is also reusable. After pouring a benzene-containing mixture onto the fabric, scientists can heat it up, vaporize the benzene and use the fabric again. Sessler and the Zhejiang University team led by Professors Feihe Huang and Guangfeng Li tested the fabric by pouring on a mixture that was 50% benzene and 50% cyclohexane. The fabric absorbed 97.9% of the benzene. For applications that require higher levels of separation, multiple passes might be used. They also demonstrated the fabric's ability to separate several other compounds of commercial interest. Sessler said that at Zhejiang University, scientists have demonstrated how to use the fabric on a larger, industrial scale. Although an economic analysis has not yet been performed, the researchers believe this could significantly reduce the amount of energy the chemical industry uses for molecular separation, with major implications for industries that manufacture paint, nylon, polyurethane and other cyclohexane-containing products. Among the study's co-authors is the late Sir Fraser Stoddart, a co-recipient of the 2016 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, who passed away before the study was complete. Publication details: Mengbin Wang et al., A two-dimensional reticular triaxial molecularly woven fabric, Nature (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11218-8
